diffs.diff: minimum supply: part 3.3 V, datasheet reading 5 V
diffs.evidence: The KY-023 has no active chip: it is two 10 kOhm potentiometers and a switch, so it is ratiometric at any supply. Product page specification table: 'Operating Voltage 3.3V–5V'; pin table: '+5V Power supply (3.3V–5V)'; FAQ 'Does the KY-023 work at 3.3V? Yes. The module operates at both 5V and 3.3V. If using a 3.3V microcontroller such as the ESP32, power the module from 3.3V'. The second reading's own source (Joy-it sensorkit KY-023) wires the module's +5V pin to '3,3 V [Pin 1]' on the Raspberry Pi and to '3,3 V' on the micro:bit. The 5 V figure (components101 'Operating Voltage: 5V', and the silkscreen label '+5V') is the nominal Arduino use, not a minimum. Running at 3.3 V is also the safe choice for 3.3 V ADCs.

diffs.diff: x_axis_volts: datasheet reading gives 1 per count, the part's model has 30.3
diffs.evidence: Different but equivalent units. The model reports X position in % of travel, with 0 % at 0 V and 100 % at Vcc = 3.3 V, so 100/3.3 = 30.3 % per volt. The second reading reports the raw wiper voltage (identity, 1 V per V). Both describe the same ratiometric divider: 'Moving the stick shifts the wiper along the resistor, changing the output voltage between 0V and VCC' (arduinomodules.info). Joy-it converts the reading the same way: '(0-1023 -> 0 V-5 V)' at 5 V and 'VRx.read_u16() * 3.3 / 65536' at 3.3 V. So the model's Vout = position x Vcc matches the source.

diffs.diff: y_axis_volts: datasheet reading gives 1 per count, the part's model has 30.3
diffs.evidence: Same as the X axis. The Y wiper is an identical 10 kOhm potentiometer, and the model's 30.3 is % of travel per volt (100 % / 3.3 V Vcc), not a different gain. The second reading gives the wiper voltage itself (1 V/V). Joy-it's Pico example converts the reading as 'yAxis = round(VRy.read_u16() * 3.3 / 65536, 2)', i.e. output 0..Vcc proportional to position, as the model has it.
